extracted.intended_audience: PR professionals, corporate communications teams, and press-release writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique checklist for writing effective press releases from a journalist's perspective, focusing on headlines, ledes, quotes, boilerplate, and verifiability. Emphasizes concrete, news-first writing and provides editing/testing recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headlines: specific with verifiable claims
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer headlines that include concrete, verifiable information rather than vague promotional language. Anti-patterns: 'no news' headlines like “Acme Corp Announces Strategic Partnership With XYZ,” buzzword soup such as “Game-Changing Innovation Disrupts Market,” and generic claims without proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline: include a specific number and concrete outcome
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a quantifiable metric (e.g., percent improvement, number of users, dollars raised) and the concrete result makes a headline newsworthy and tangible. Test whether the number is verifiable and meaningful to the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline: name recognizable entities
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include well-known customers, partners, or other named entities when possible to increase relevance and credibility. Avoid anonymity or generic references that reduce news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline: include clear timeframe when applicable
rubrics_metrics.description: Timeframe ('by end of year', 'in next 90 days')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adding a timeframe grounds the claim and increases newsworthiness; ensure the timeframe is accurate and verifiable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline: substantiate any 'first' or superlative claims
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims like 'industry-first' must be verifiable. Avoid unsubstantiated superlatives and be prepared to document uniqueness or precedence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede: news-first and front-loaded
rubrics_metrics.description: Front-loaded news in 50 words or less
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with the core news (who/what/when/where/why/how) within about 50 words. Avoid throat-clearing ledes such as 'Today, Acme Corp is excited to announce...' which delay the actual news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede: provide a concrete proof point quickly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediately follow the news hook with a specific evidence or metric that supports the news claim (e.g., customer metric, study result). This reduces promotional vagueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede: make the stakes clear for the reader
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why the news matters to the audience—what changes or impacts result—so readers/journalists understand relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lede: compress the 5 W's while remaining complete
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure who, what, when, where, and why are present and compressed tightly into the opening so editors can quickly assess news value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotes: substantive and human
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes should add insight, personality, or explanation rather than generic praise. Avoid bland, promotional quotes that add no information ('We are excited to bring this to market').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote: include specific reasoning behind decisions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good quote explains why a decision was made or what strategic thinking underlies the announcement, giving reporters useful color and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote: provide counter-intuitive or surprising insight
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotes that reveal an unexpected perspective or nuance are more likely to be used and make the piece more interesting to journalists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote: acknowledge tradeoffs or limitations honestly
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human, credible quotes may admit constraints or tradeoffs, which adds believability and journalistic value compared with overhyped claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote: use customer testimonials with metrics
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customer quotes that include concrete metrics (e.g., 'reduced costs by 30%') are more compelling and verifiable than vague endorsements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quote: avoid obviously ghostwritten or canned statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote attributed to executive who clearly didn't write it
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure quotes sound like the speaker and include details they could credibly provide; otherwise reporters may view them as inauthentic and unused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boilerplate: concise and factual
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep company descriptions short and factual. Anti-patterns: 200+ word company descriptions, clichéd phrases like 'leading provider of solutions' or 'industry leader in innovation' that offer no verifiable detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: All claims must be verifiable
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every factual or numerical claim in the release should be checkable. Verify statistics, 'first' claims, and other assertions before distribution to avoid embarrassment and loss of credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing: cut adjectives and adverbs after first draft
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut every adjective and adverb after first draft
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim promotional modifiers to sharpen prose and reduce puffery. This helps the release sound more factual and less like marketing copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing: read the release aloud to test flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Read aloud to test for flow
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reading aloud reveals awkward phrasing, repetition, and throat-clearing language that may not be obvious on the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review: have an outside reader review
rubrics_metrics.description: Have outside reader (not in marketing) review
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Get feedback from someone outside the marketing team—ideally a journalist or a non-marketing colleague—to ensure clarity and newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline test: 'would I tweet this?' filter
rubrics_metrics.description: Test headline with 'would I tweet this?' filter
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a quick social-share heuristic to see if the headline is punchy and clear enough to stand alone; if it wouldn’t make you click/retweet, rework it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify numerical claims separately
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double- and triple-check numbers and their sources. This is called out separately as a repeated recommendation and mirrors 'all claims verifiable' but emphasizes quantitative accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid marketing language in boilerplate and copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Marketing language instead of factual description
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace promotional jargon with specific facts about products, customers, history, or measurable outcomes to improve credibility and journalist utility.
